claims.text: The balance between a predominant FCC matrix and a controlled amount of ordered B2 or BCC/B2 phase governs phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
A strong negative mixing enthalpy between Ni and Al drives local Ni–Al chemical ordering.
Ni–Al ordering produces coherent nanoscale B2 or ordered-BCC precipitates within an FCC matrix.
The ordered precipitates hinder dislocation motion and thereby increase high-temperature strength.
The precipitate/matrix interfaces act as irradiation-defect sinks.
Defect absorption by the precipitate/matrix interfaces improves radiation tolerance.
A limited B2 fraction preserves the ductility of the retained FCC matrix.
Retaining a ductile FCC matrix maintains or improves cryogenic toughness.
A controlled FCC+B2 alloy will have greater high-temperature strength than a fully FCC baseline.
A controlled FCC+B2 alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density or better post-irradiation recovery than a fully FCC baseline.
An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy can be prepared in a single-phase FCC state for use as the baseline.
An isothermal treatment within 900–1150 °C can promote a limited coherent B2 phase without fully transforming the FCC matrix.
Increasing the Ni-to-Al ratio promotes nucleation and growth of a Ni–Al-rich B2 phase.
Processing can change the relative fractions of FCC and BCC/B2 phases.
Overall phase stability reflects competition between entropy stabilization of FCC and the energetic favorability of Ni–Al ordering.
The hypothesis is restricted to limited Ni and Al adjustments and processing conditions that produce B2 onset without B2 dominance.
XRD, EBSD, and EDS can quantify the B2 precipitate fraction, size, and distribution in the proposed comparison.
The optimal B2 volume fraction, precipitate size, and spatial distribution have not been quantitatively established.
Interactions with carbides, oxides, and other secondary phases remain unresolved.

contradictions.description: The baseline is said to be processed under identical conditions, but the falsification experiment assigns different heat treatments to suppress versus promote B2 precipitation. The intended controlled variables therefore are not consistently specified.

The hypothesis only requires preservation or maintenance of cryogenic toughness, and the prediction allows maintained or improved toughness, whereas the falsification rule requires a statistically significant enhancement in cryogenic toughness. A result that maintains toughness would satisfy the prediction but could trigger the stated falsification rule.
